documentNotes.title: Native editorial preface
documentNotes.statement:
Preface
Preface
Preface
Preface 
This publication contains the competition problems (Volume 2) from the 21st – 40th 
International Chemistry Olympiads (IChO) organized in the years 1989 – 2008  and is a 
continuation of the publication that appeared last year as Volume 1 and contained 
competition problems from the first twenty IChOs.  The whole review of the competition 
tasks set in the IChO in its fourty-year history is a contribution of the IChO International 
Information Centre in Bratislava (Slovakia) to the development of this world known 
international competition. This Volume 2 contains 154 theoretical and 46 practical 
competition problems from the mentioned years. The review as a whole presents 
altogether 279 theoretical and 96 practical problems.  
In the elaboration of this collection the editor had to face certain difficulties because 
the aim was not only to make use of past recordings but also to give them such a form 
that they may be used in practice and further chemical education. Consequently, it was 
necessary to make some corrections in order to unify the form of the problems. However, 
they did not concern the contents and language of the problems.  
Unfortunately, the authors of the particular competition problems are not known and 
due to the procedure of the creation of the IChO competition problems, it is impossible to 
assign any author's name to a particular problem. As the editor I would appreciate many  
times some discussion with the authors about any critical places that occurred in the text. 
On the other hand, any additional amendments to the text would be not correct from the  
historical point of view. Therefore, responsibility for the scientific content and language of 
the problems lies exclusively with the organizers of the particular International Chemistry 
Olympiads.    
 
Some parts of texts, especially those gained as scanned materials, could not be 
used directly and thus, several texts, schemes and pictures had to be re-written or created 
again. Some solutions were often available in a brief form and necessary extent only, just 
for the needs of members of the International Jury.  
 
Recalculations of the solutions were made in some special cases only when the 
numeric results in the original solutions showed to be obviously not correct. Although the 
numbers of significant figures in the results of several solutions do not obey the criteria 
generally accepted, they were left without change.      


 
In this publication SI quantities and units are used and a more modern method of 
chemical calculations is introduced. Only some exceptions have been made when, in an 
effort to preserve the original text, the quantities and units have been used that are not SI.  
There were some problems with the presentation of the solutions of practical tasks, 
because most of the relatively simple calculations were based on the experimental results 
of contestants. Moreover, the practical problems are accompanied with answer sheets in 
the last years and several additional questions and tasks have appeared in them that were 
not a part of the text of the original experimental problems. Naturally, answer sheets could 
not be included in this publication and can only be preserved as archive materials. 
  
When reading the texts of the IChO problems one must admire and appreciate the 
work of those many known and unknown people – teachers, authors, pupils, and 
organizers – who contributed so much to development and success of this important 
international competition. 
 
I am sure about the usefulness of the this review of the IChO problems. It may serve 
not only as archive material but, in particular, this review should serve to both competitors 
and their teachers as a source of further inspiration in their preparation for this challenging 
competition. 
 
 
 
 
Bratislava, July 2009  
 
 
 
 
 
 
  
 
                                    Anton Sirota, editor

problems.title: A Kinetic Study of the Acid Catalyzed Reaction Between Acetone and Iodine in Aqueous Solution
problems.statement:
The reaction between acetone and iodine in aqueous solution is catalyzed by H⁺.

$$
\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3(aq)+I_2(aq)}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{H^+}}
\mathrm{CH_3COCH_2I(aq)+H^+(aq)+I^-(aq)}.
$$

The rate law for this reaction is:

$$
-\frac{d[\mathrm{I_2}]}{dt}=k[\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}]^x[\mathrm{I_2}]^y[\mathrm{H^+}]^z,\qquad
v_0=k[\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}]_0^x[\mathrm{I_2}]_0^y[\mathrm{H^+}]_0^z.
$$

where H⁺ ions are the catalyst. In order to determine the rate constant $k$ and the kinetic orders $x$, $y$, $z$, the initial rate of reaction is measured, where $[\,]_0$ are the initial concentrations of acetone, I₂ and H⁺, respectively.

If the initial rates are measured for various initial concentrations of the reactants then the order with respect to each reactant can be obtained.

The initial rate is obtained by measuring the decrease in the I₂(aq) concentration after a short time interval (7.0 min. in this experiment) after the start of the reaction. Aqueous sodium acetate solution is added to stop the reaction after 7 minutes. The acetate ion reacts immediately with the H⁺ to produce acetic acid and so reducing the concentration of H⁺. The reaction is thus stopped as there is no catalyst present.

Since the reaction does not come to a complete halt, the solution should be titrated immediately after the addition of the sodium acetate solution.

The remaining iodine I₂(aq) is determined by titration with sodium thiosulphate, Na₂S₂O₃. As the end point of the titration is approached, starch indicator is added and the titration is continued until the blue colour disappears.

sections.statement:
| Supplied chemical | Quantity |

parts.statement: Pipette 5.00 cm³ aqueous iodine into a clean 125 cm³ Erlenmeyer flask.
Add 10 cm³ distilled water using a graduated cylinder.
Titrate with standard 0.02 M sodium thiosulphate until pale yellow.
Add 3–4 drops starch; continue until blue disappears.
Record initial/final thiosulphate volumes and volume used on the answer sheet.
Repeat steps 1–5 as necessary.
Give the titre used for calculation on the answer sheet.
Calculate iodine concentration.
Label stoppered flasks I–IV.

Add these volumes, in cm³, and stopper each flask immediately.

| Flask | Water | 0.100 M HCl | 50% acetone |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| I | 5.00 | 5.00 | 5.00 |
| II | 0.0 | 5.00 | 5.00 |
| III | 0.0 | 5.00 | 10.00 |
| IV | 0.0 | 10.00 | 5.00 |
Measure 10 cm³ of 0.50 M sodium acetate in a graduated cylinder.
Set the stopwatch to 0.0000.
Pipette 5.00 cm³ iodine into flask I. Start timing as its first drop is added.
Stopper and swirl continuously.
Remove stopper just before 7.0 min. At 7.0 min immediately pour in the measured 10 cm³ sodium acetate; shake well.
Titrate remaining iodine with standard thiosulphate.
Record thiosulphate volume.
Repeat steps 3–9 for II–IV, using iodine volumes 10.00, 5.00 and 5.00 cm³ respectively at step 5.

**(B-1)**


Calculate initial molar concentrations of iodine, acetone and HCl in I–IV, assuming additive volumes.

**(B-2)**


Calculate iodine concentrations remaining after 7.0 min.

**(B-3)**


Calculate initial reaction rates in M s⁻¹.

**(B-4)**


The rate law is $-d[\mathrm{I_2}]/dt=k[\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}]^x[\mathrm{I_2}]^y[\mathrm{H^+}]^z$. Calculate $x,y,z$ from rates and initial concentrations; round to nearest integers and fill the answer sheet. Write the rate equation.

**(B-5)**


Calculate each flask's rate constant with proper units.

**(B-6)**


Give the mean rate constant.

solution.statement:
In A, competitors use the bottle's standard thiosulphate concentration and their titres to calculate iodine concentration. Results were expected in an answer-sheet table. In B the collection lists calculations B1–B5:

- B1: initial concentrations in mixtures.
- B2: remaining iodine concentration at seven minutes.
- B3: initial iodine disappearance rate,

$$
-\frac{d[\mathrm{I_2}]}{dt}=\frac{c(\mathrm{I_2})_{\mathrm{initial}}-c(\mathrm{I_2})_{7\mathrm{min}}}{7\times60\ \mathrm{s}}.
$$

- B4: compare II:I, III:I and IV:I to find **$x=1,y=0,z=1$**, giving $v=k[\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}][\mathrm{H^+}]$.
- B5: calculate each mixture's rate constant and their mean.

problems.title: Isolation and Identification of an Essential Oil from Natural Source
problems.statement: Steam-distil a supplied natural source, determine the main essential oil **S**, and identify a product **Y** of its chemical conversion. Use organic qualitative tests to identify functional groups with the station's reagents. NMR data will be given **only after** functional-group tests are complete.

sections.title: Chemicals available
sections.statement: A 1 g sample in a vial; unknown Y in a vial; anhydrous sodium sulphate in a plastic vial; dichloromethane; ceric ammonium nitrate solution; 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine labelled “2,4-DNP”; 2% aqueous ammonia; 5% aqueous silver nitrate, HCl, NaOH and sodium bicarbonate; 1% iron(III) chloride in ethanol; 0.2% aqueous potassium permanganate, decolourized by easily oxidized groups; acetone for washing.

parts.statement:
**Apparatus:** assemble a distillation apparatus with a 25 cm³ round-bottomed distilling flask and 10 cm³ round-bottomed receiver. Heat sand bath to approximately $150\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ before the next step.

**Simplified steam distillation:** mix 1 g ground sample with 15 cm³ water in the 25 cm³ flask; soak about ten minutes. Add a magnetic stirrer bar, turn on condenser water and stirring motor. Heat for a steady distillation rate, with sand bath not below $170\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Collect at least 5 cm³ distillate. Turn off the hotplate, dismantle and rinse condenser with acetone. Ensure it is dry before reuse.

**Extraction:** transfer distillate to a capped 15 cm³ centrifuge tube. Add 1 cm³ dichloromethane; cap securely, shake vigorously, and cool in ice. Allow layers to separate. Transfer dichloromethane with a Pasteur pipette to a 10 cm³ test tube. Repeat twice with fresh 1 cm³ portions and combine all extracts.

**Drying:** add anhydrous $\mathrm{Na_2SO_4}$; stir occasionally for ten minutes.

**Evaporation:** with a clean dry cotton-plugged Pasteur pipette transfer organic liquid to a dry 5 cm³ conical vial. Wash the sulphate with approximately 1 cm³ clean dichloromethane and transfer the wash, without carrying sulphate into the vial. Use a Hickman still head and dry condenser to distil dichloromethane until 1 cm³ remains. Remove distilled solvent from the head with a pipette or syringe to the recovered-dichloromethane vial. Keep residue for tests.

**Functional-group analysis:** test the 1 cm³ residue with suitable station reagents. Dichloromethane is immiscible with water.

**Tollen’s Reagent:** add one drop 5% aqueous silver nitrate and one drop 5% aqueous NaOH to a small test tube. A brown precipitate appears. Add 2% aqueous ammonia until it all dissolves; the solution is ready.
Elucidate S. Reaction with $\mathrm{CH_3I/K_2CO_3}$ gives **X**, $\mathrm{C_{11}H_{14}O_2}$. Oxidation of X gives **Y**, $\mathrm{C_{10}H_{12}O_4}$, as the main product, and carbon dioxide.

Identify Y's functional groups with station reagents. Fill the answer sheet and state which groups are present or absent. Hand in Part I (Demonstrator copy) and ask for $^1\mathrm{H}$ NMR spectra, supplied only after these tests are completed.
Draw the main distilled essential-oil structure S. Assign every proton from the supplied $^1\mathrm{H}$ NMR by labelling peak numbers on the answer-sheet structure.
Draw X and Y. Assign each Y proton from the supplied NMR in the same manner.
